Words and actions, of course, have some limitations, such as active discrimination, slander, harassment, inciting riots, etc. But the essence of free speech, as I've understood it anyway, is that no one should have to fear being assaulted, jailed, or exiled just because of something they've said that is merely an expression of their thoughts and beliefs.

I'm in an unpopular group: white male Trump supporter, non-politically correct, atheist, race-realist with pretty traditional values and morals. Five years ago I'd have said this unapologetically. Now, honestly, I feel like even posting that fact on voat could get me in trouble some day. And I've never committed a crime against anyone or hurt anyone based on my views.

But the essence of free speech, as I've understood it anyway, is that no one should have to fear being assaulted, jailed, or exiled just because of something they've said that is merely an expression of their thoughts and beliefs

Sounds about right, but.. more specifically, free speech is about governments/rulers not punishing you for saying something they don't like. That's what really matters, and everything else is basically just a distraction.

What if someone yells "Fire!" in a crowded theater (when there is no fire)? -Well he's being a fuckwad and certainly deserves some negative consequences, but people conflate the idea of someone doing that with say, a Russian journalist criticizing Putin even though they're vastly different things.

The level of freedom of our speech is inversely correlated with the level of authoritarianism of our governments.

What will a dictator do to a journalist who criticizes him? -Well he's going to have him imprisoned (and beaten? tortured? etc), but the goal there is to make an example of him, so that others would refrain from saying things that the dictator doesn't like.

What happens in Game of Thrones when someone criticizes the King? -Why that would be the same thing. That's how political authority works - someone has the perceived (not real) right to impose his will on everyone else, by force if "necessary", and anyone who resists will be made an example of, so that others wouldn't get similar ideas.. and thus, political authority is maintained.

Free speech is essentially the idea that you can say things your rulers don't like, without suffering negative consequences for it. But try exposing serious wrongdoing like Bradley Manning, and.. you end up serving as an Example.

Try being a mainstream media journalist who actually does what he's supposed to, like Michael Hastings, and you'll find your car becoming uncontrollable and its engine exploding..

You see, even when you have "free speech", you still have rulers, and whenever you pose a serious enough threat to them, you will be neutralized one way or another..

The moral of the story here is that we should not have rulers, which means there should be no political power or authority at all, and by extension, no governments.

So in a way, free speech itself is just a distraction. What we really want is actual freedom, not ideas that make us more comfortable with having rulers.
